report.summary: (model supplied no summary; its answer is preserved in handoff)

handoff.purpose: Implement fan_out() to execute tasks concurrently, enforce spend guard and temperature/votes policy, and return a uniform run summary.

symbols.name: fan_out
symbols.note: Main entry point; runs tasks, writes result JSONs, installs process guard, returns dict summary.

claims.text: Run every task, land every answer, return the run summary.
claims.why: The function loops through all tasks via ThreadPoolExecutor, writes a result file per task, and returns a summary dict.

claims.text: Never raises for a failing task: a fan-out of 1,200 in which one task dies must produce 1,199 answers and a named failure, not an exception.
claims.why: Exceptions inside _run_task are caught per vote and appended to res.errors; exceptions from fut.result() are caught in the loop and turned into a FanoutResult with errors. The only uncaught exceptions are from setup (guard, trace) which are handled and return 'refused'.

claims.text: Transport failures are recorded on the result and the queue continues -- which is also why the summary reports 'failed' separately from 'ok' rather than folding them into a rate.
claims.why: Exceptions in _run_task are caught and recorded in res.errors; the summary counts failed separately from ok and blocked.

claims.text: 'resume' skips any task whose result file already exists AND parses.
claims.why: In _run_task, if resume is True and dest.is_file(), it reads and json.loads the file; if that succeeds and the result is not blocked with answers, it returns the prior result.

claims.text: A file that exists but does not parse is re-run, because a truncated result is worse than a missing one: it looks like an answer.
claims.why: The except (OSError, ValueError) catches JSON decode errors and file read errors, then falls through to re-run the task.

claims.text: At temperature 0.0 the decode is deterministic, so every vote returns the SAME answer and the agreement it produces is an artefact of counting one answer N times.
claims.why: The code refuses when any task has votes>1 and temperature<=0.0, treating it as a policy violation. The comment's claim about determinism is consistent with the refusal logic.

claims.text: asking for votes you cannot get is an error at the door, where it costs nothing, rather than a dataset that has to be thrown away later.
claims.why: The check occurs before any calls are made, returning a 'refused' summary with no paid calls.

claims.text: Fail CLOSED: a fan-out whose spend cannot be capped does not run.
claims.why: If install_process_guard() raises, the function returns a 'refused' summary with paid_calls=0.

claims.text: SAME SUMMARY SHAPE as a completed run, including 'paid_calls' and 'results'.
claims.why: The refused return dict includes keys: state, reason, tasks, ok, blocked, failed, resumed, paid_calls, out_dir, concurrency, results -- matching the success return shape.

claims.text: Resolved ONCE for the whole fan-out: every answer in one run belongs to that run.
claims.why: trace = current_trace_id() is called once before the thread pool and passed to every FanoutResult.

claims.text: Imported here rather than at module scope for the same reason the provider is -- a caller reading the dataclasses should not pull the spine.
claims.why: The import is inside the function, so importing fanout does not import the spine module.

claims.text: NOT re-stamped: the prior trace is the run that paid for this answer. Overwriting it with the current run's id would claim this run produced something it read off disk.
claims.why: The code sets trace_id=prior.get('trace_id') rather than the current trace.

claims.text: An all-blocked result is NOT servable. ... Serving it forever was measured 2026-07-31: the claims123 review tier's 6 blocked units would have been replayed into every future run as if they had been audited.
claims.why: The resume branch only returns the prior result if res.answers and not res.blocked; otherwise it re-runs.

claims.text: ok / blocked / failed are DISJOINT: 'ok' now means the unit produced at least one answer carrying evidence. Folding refusals into ok was measured reading 'ok=6' on a tier whose every unit had been refused.
claims.why: The counting uses if res.blocked, elif res.ok, else failed, ensuring disjoint categories.

claims.text: PAID CALLS, separate from task count: with votes>1 they differ, and the number anyone asking 'what did this cost' wants is this one.
claims.why: counts['calls'] is incremented per vote inside _run_task, so with votes>1 it exceeds the task count.

claims.text: it is a COUNT -- the budget ledger prices reservations at a deliberate worst-case, so a ledger total is a ceiling and never an invoice.
claims.why: The code returns counts['calls'] as paid_calls, which is a count of actual calls made, not a ledger total; the comment's claim about the ledger is uncheckable here but the count is as described.

claims.text: a refusal that returns a different dict forces every consumer to write two code paths, and the one it will forget is the refusal -- so a caller reading 'paid_calls' would crash exactly when the answer it needed was 'zero, nothing was spent'.
claims.why: The refused return includes paid_calls=0 and the same keys as success, so callers can read the same fields.

observations.what: The 'refused' summary for guard failure and for temperature/votes violation both use the same shape, but the temperature/votes refusal omits 'reason' in the same way? Actually both include 'reason'. No issue.

The 'refused' summary for guard failure and for temperature/votes violation both use the same shape, but the temperature/votes refusal omits 'reason' in the same way? Actually both include 'reason'. No issue.

The function installs the process guard via a deferred import from ..budget. If that module is missing or has import errors, the guard fails and the run is refused. This is by design (fail closed), but the import is not pinned to a specific module path beyond '..budget'. No defect.
The trace_id is obtained once and used for all results, but in the resume branch it is overridden by the prior trace. That is intentional per the comment. No defect.

The counting of 'calls' is incremented inside _run_task under a lock, but the lock is also used for appending results and counting ok/blocked/failed. There is a potential race: the 'calls' counter is incremented per vote, but the summary counts ok/blocked/failed per result after the whole task completes. Since each task is submitted as a unit, the counters are updated under lock, but the 'calls' counter is incremented inside the vote loop before the result is appended. This means that at the time a result is appended, the 'calls' count may not yet include all votes of that task if the task is still running? Actually no: _run_task does not return until all votes are done, so the increment of 'calls' for a task happens before the result is appended (the result is appended after the task completes). However, the increment happens inside the loop, so if the task has multiple votes, the 'calls' count is incremented multiple times under lock, but the result is only appended after the loop. So the final summary will have the correct count. The progress print reads counts['calls'] under the same lock? It reads it after acquiring the lock? Actually the print is outside the lock, but it reads counts['calls'] which is only modified under lock. There is a potential race: the print could read a stale value, but that is cosmetic. No defect.

The 'resume' check reads the destination file with dest.read_text() and json.loads. If the file is large or the JSON is huge, this could be slow, but no defect. The exception handling catches OSError and ValueError, but not other exceptions like TypeError from json.loads? Actually json.loads can raise JSONDecodeError which is a subclass of ValueError, so it is caught. No defect.
The function returns a dict with 'results' as a list of dicts via to_dict(). The on_result callback is called with the FanoutResult object, not the dict. No defect.

The temperature/votes refusal returns 'state': 'refused' but the docstring does not mention that a refusal can happen for this reason. The docstring says 'Never raises for a failing task' but does not mention that the whole run can be refused before starting. This is a documentation gap, but not a code defect.

The guard installation is done inside a try/except that catches all exceptions, but if the import of install_process_guard fails (e.g., ImportError), it is caught and the run is refused. That is fail-closed. No defect.
The 'refused' summary for guard failure includes 'reason' with the guard error, but the temperature/votes refusal includes a long reason. Both are fine.

risks: line 353 | low | Deferred import of install_process_guard from ..budget; if that module has a typo or missing symbol, the run is refused (fail closed) but the error message may be cryptic. What would settle it: check that ..budget defines install_process_guard and that its import has no side effects that break when imported lazily.

line 380-398 | low | Resume path reads and parses the entire result file; a malformed JSON raises ValueError and is caught, but a very large file could cause memory pressure. What would settle it: check if any result file can be arbitrarily large; consider streaming or size limits.
